short_history: Ace Tone, formally Ace Electronic Industries Inc., was a Japanese manufacturer of organs, amplifiers, effects units and drum machines, founded in Osaka in 1960 by engineer Ikutaro Kakehashi with backing from the trading company Sakata Shokai. Its best-known product was the Rhythm Ace line of preset drum machines, starting with the six-button R1 in 1964 and reaching commercial success with the FR-1 in 1967, which led to a business partnership with the Hammond Organ Company. In 1972 Kakehashi left to found Roland Corporation, and Ace Tone itself was folded into a Hammond and Sakata Shokai joint venture called Nihon Hammond soon after, ending the Ace Tone brand as an independent line. Roland's earliest drum machines directly reused Ace Tone circuit designs, making Ace Tone the acknowledged forerunner of Roland even though the two companies were never formally merged.
long_history: Ikutaro Kakehashi (1930-2017) began repairing radios and electronics in Osaka in the 1950s after recovering from tuberculosis, and by the late 1950s was experimenting with building his own electric organ from spare parts. He formally founded Ace Electronic Industries Inc., trading as Ace Tone, in Osaka in 1960 with investment from the trading house Sakata Shokai, initially building amplifiers before moving into electronic organs, some of which were sold as OEM products under the Matsushita/Panasonic and National brands. In 1964 Kakehashi unveiled the R1 Rhythm Ace at the NAMM Show, a transistorized six-button percussion instrument regarded as one of the earliest fully electronic drum devices, though it sold poorly because it lacked automatic accompaniment patterns. Ace Tone set up US distribution through the Sorkin company in 1965, and in 1967 launched the FR-1 Rhythm Ace, which added automatically triggered preset rhythm patterns and variable tempo; the FR-1 was a commercial hit and led to a partnership with the American organ maker Hammond. Through the late 1960s and early 1970s Ace Tone expanded into combo and home organs (the TOP and GT series, the X-3), electric pianos (AP-100), synthesizers (the Multistrings SY-5, PS-1000 and SY-100), guitar effects including fuzz boxes and echo units, and a wide range of guitar and bass amplifiers, PA mixers and microphones, sold partly under other brand names such as Multivox. Kakehashi left the company in 1972 to found Roland Corporation; not long after, Ace Electronic Industries was restructured into Nihon Hammond, a joint venture between the Hammond Organ Company and Sakata Shokai, and the Ace Tone name faded from the market. Roland's own first drum machines, the Rhythm 33 and Rhythm 77, were direct descendants of Ace Tone's FR-3L and FR-7L models, cementing Ace Tone's reputation as Roland's direct technical and commercial ancestor, though the sources reviewed describe no formal corporate merger or acquisition linking the two companies.

short_history: Music-production division spun out in 1984 from the Japanese consumer-electronics maker Akai (founded 1929); developed the influential MPC sampler/sequencer line with engineer Roger Linn starting in 1988, became fully independent from its parent in 1999, and has been part of inMusic Brands since a 2005 acquisition.
long_history: Akai Electric Co., Ltd. was founded in Tokyo in 1929 by Masukichi Akai and his son Saburo, and became internationally known for tape recorders through the 1960s-70s. In 1984 the company spun out a dedicated music-production division, Akai Professional, focused on synthesizers and samplers. Working with engineer Roger Linn, Akai Professional released the MPC60 in 1988, combining a 12-bit sampler, sequencer and the now-iconic 4x4 velocity-sensitive pad grid; the MPC line went on to shape the sound of hip-hop production for artists including Dr. Dre and J Dilla. Akai Professional separated into an independent business in 1999, while its parent company went through a series of ownership changes (Mitsubishi Electric, then International Semi-Tech Microsystems) before the wider Akai Holdings group filed for insolvency in 2000 and passed to Hong Kong's Grande Holdings. Akai Professional itself was acquired in 2005 by businessman Jack O'Donnell and is now part of his inMusic Brands group, continuing to develop MPC hardware and other production instruments.

short_history: American audio-technology company founded in 1984 by Keith Barr, initially known for digital effects units and the ADAT multitrack recorder, that entered synthesizers in 2000 with the analog Andromeda A6 and the Ion virtual-analog synth before financial trouble in 2001 led to acquisition and eventual ownership by inMusic Brands.
long_history: Keith Barr, previously a principal at guitar-effects maker MXR, founded Alesis in 1984, choosing the name to evoke Algorithmic Electronic Systems. The company built its early reputation on affordable digital signal processing: the 1985 XT Reverb undercut competitors at $799, and the 1986 MIDIverb became one of the first widely affordable MIDI-controllable effects units. Its most influential product was the 1991 ADAT, the first multitrack digital tape recorder priced within reach of home and project studios, which reshaped affordable recording. Alesis moved into synthesizers around 2000, using its custom IC design expertise to build the Andromeda A6, among the last large-scale polyphonic analog synthesizers to reach mass production, followed by the virtual-analog Ion. The company went through bankruptcy in 2001 and was acquired by Jack O'Donnell; it has not released a new synth design since the 2005 Fusion. Alesis is now a brand of inMusic Brands and continues to make drum machines, interfaces and controllers, headquartered in Cumberland, Rhode Island.

short_history: Founded in 1969 in Lexington, Massachusetts by engineer Alan R. Pearlman, initially as Tonus, Inc., before adopting the ARP name (from his own initials). Became a dominant force in 1970s synthesizers, at one point holding roughly 40% of the market, with instruments like the ARP 2600 and Odyssey. A costly, underperforming guitar-synthesizer project drained the company's finances, and ARP was forced into bankruptcy in 1981; its assets, including the prototype ARP Chroma, were sold to CBS Musical Instruments and the Chroma was later released as the Rhodes Chroma.
long_history: ARP Instruments was founded in Lexington, Massachusetts in 1969 by Alan R. Pearlman, an electrical engineer who had previously co-founded and sold an amplifier company, Nexus Research Labs, giving him the capital to start a synthesizer venture on his own terms. The company was initially incorporated as Tonus, Inc. before taking the ARP name, derived from Pearlman's own initials. Through the 1970s ARP became one of the two dominant American synthesizer makers alongside Moog, producing widely used instruments such as the ARP 2600 (a semi-modular synth popular in both studios and education) and the more affordable, best-selling ARP Odyssey, at one point capturing roughly 40 percent of the synthesizer market. The company's decline began in 1977, when it committed heavily to developing the ARP Avatar, a guitar synthesizer, against Pearlman's own objections. The Avatar arrived late, worked poorly, and consumed about four million dollars in development and production costs against roughly one million dollars in sales over two years, crippling the company's cash flow and starving other product development. With sales declining and no major new product to rely on, ARP was pushed into bankruptcy in 1981 after a bank called in an outstanding loan; a court-appointed trustee liquidated the company's assets later that year. Among the assets sold was the prototype for a new polyphonic synthesizer, the ARP Chroma, which CBS Musical Instruments purchased along with other ARP assets for $350,000; CBS ultimately brought the instrument to market under its own Rhodes brand as the Rhodes Chroma rather than the ARP name.

short_history: German audio-electronics company founded in 1989 by Uli Behringer, built on affordable processors and mixers before manufacturing shifted to China from 1997; entered synthesizers in 2016 with the Model D (a Minimoog clone) and has since released many analog and digital synth clones, operating today under the Music Tribe corporate umbrella alongside brands like Midas and TC Electronic.
long_history: Uli Behringer, who built his first synthesizer (the UB1) at age 16, founded the company in Willich, Germany on 25 January 1989, starting with an Aural Exciter and a compressor designed around his own kitchen table. Early growth came from affordable studio processors, and in 1997 the company began moving manufacturing to China, opening its first large Chinese factory in 2002. Through the 2000s and 2010s the parent structure (renamed Music Group, then Music Tribe in 2017) acquired a string of established audio brands, including Midas and Klark Teknik (2009), Turbosound (2012), TC Group/TC Electronic/TC-Helicon (2015), Tannoy, and Aston Microphones. Behringer's own entry into synthesizers came later than its mixer and interface business: the 2016 Model D, a faithful clone of the Minimoog, marked the brand's serious arrival in the synth market, followed by many further analog and digital clone and original instruments. Music Tribe is today based in Manila, the Philippines, with its main manufacturing complex, Music Tribe City, in Zhongshan, China.

short_history: Founded in 1963 in Berkeley, California, by synthesizer pioneer Don Buchla as Buchla & Associates, producing one of the earliest modular voltage-controlled synthesizer systems alongside Robert Moog's parallel work. Buchla avoided the term "synthesizer", favoring instruments built for original sound design over imitating existing instruments. Australian investors acquired the company in 2012 and renamed it Buchla Electronic Musical Instruments; after Don Buchla's death in 2016, the assets passed to Buchla U.S.A. in 2018, which continues production today.
long_history: Don Buchla built his first modular system in 1963 on commission from composers Morton Subotnick and Ramon Sender at the San Francisco Tape Music Center, funded by a Rockefeller Foundation grant; the resulting Buchla 100 series was installed at the Tape Music Center in 1965 and moved to Mills College in 1966. It became one of the two foundational voltage-controlled synthesizer designs of the era alongside Robert Moog's instruments, and was used on landmark early electronic works including Subotnick's "Silver Apples of the Moon" and Buffy Sainte-Marie's 1969 album "Illuminations". The 200 series ("Electric Music Box", 1970) expanded the control capabilities, and later computer-integrated systems (the 300, 400, 500 and 700 series through the mid-1970s and 1980s) brought digital control to the modular format. In the late 1980s Buchla also built MIDI controllers (Thunder, Lightning, Marimba Lumina), and returned to the modular format with the hybrid analog-digital 200e series in 2004. Throughout, Buchla's design philosophy centered on complex oscillators, vactrol-based circuits and unconventional performance interfaces intended to generate genuinely new sounds rather than imitate acoustic instruments. Ownership passed from Buchla himself to a group of Australian investors (Audio Supermarket Pty Ltd) in 2012, who renamed the company Buchla Electronic Musical Instruments; Don Buchla died in September 2016, and in 2018 the company's assets were acquired by a new entity, Buchla U.S.A., under which production continues.

short_history: Crumar was an Italian maker of electronic organs, string machines and analog synthesizers, founded in Castelfidardo in the late 1960s by Mario Crucianelli together with a business partner named Marchetti, whose surnames were blended to create the brand name. Through the 1970s the company built organs and string and piano synthesizers before moving into fuller synthesizer designs, culminating in respected models such as the DS-2, the Bob Moog-designed Spirit, and the DCO-based Bit One, Bit 01 and Bit 99 polysynths of the mid-1980s. Competition from Japanese digital keyboard makers pushed the original company out of business in the mid-to-late 1980s. In 2008 the Crumar name was revived as a new Italian company, and it now sells digital organs, stage pianos and occasional reissues of classic models under the original brand.
long_history: Crumar traces back to Castelfidardo, a historic Italian hub for accordion and electronic-instrument manufacturing. It grew out of Mario Crucianelli's existing accordion business, and the Crumar name was formed by combining syllables of 'Crucianelli' and 'Marchetti', the surname of a business partner. Through the early-to-mid 1970s Crumar's catalogue centred on electric pianos and string synthesizers, including the Compac-piano, Compac-string, Pianoman, Stringman and Multiman lines, alongside the Organizer series of drawbar organs built between 1974 and 1981 and the Performer analog strings-and-brass synth. In 1978 Crumar released the DS-2, notable for using one of the earliest digitally controlled oscillator designs in a synthesizer. The company also partnered with the New York firm Music Technology Inc. to help produce the GDS and later the Digital Keyboards Synergy digital synthesizers. In 1983 Crumar released the monophonic Spirit, designed in collaboration with Minimoog co-designer Bob Moog and engineer Jim Scott; it became one of the brand's most sought-after instruments and was used by artists including Sun Ra. In 1984 and 1985 Crumar launched the Bit series, comprising the Bit One synth, the Bit 01 rack expander and the Bit 99 keyboard version, six-voice analog polysynths with two DCOs per voice and MIDI, which in the US were also sold under the name 'Unique DBE'. Despite this innovation, the rise of cheaper, more powerful Japanese digital synthesizers such as the Yamaha DX7 eroded Crumar's market, and the original company declared bankruptcy and wound down operations in the second half of the 1980s; one account describes the winding-down as a gradual sale of projects and business units rather than a single closure event. The brand lay dormant until 2008, when it was reformed as a new Italian company; sources name Andrea Agnoletto as the owner who revived it, while another account credits a 2009 acquisition by a firm called V.M. Connection, and it is unclear whether these are the same entity, a rename or sequential owners. Since then Crumar has released digital organs including the Mojo clonewheel line, stage pianos such as the DK61, Sorrento, BURN and Seven, and limited-run analog reissues, among them a 100-unit run of the Spirit reissued in 2023 that has since sold out.

short_history: German modular-synthesizer maker founded in 1979 by Dieter Doepfer near Munich, best known for introducing the A-100 system in 1995-96, whose 3U/HP module standard became the Eurorack format that is now the dominant modular synthesizer standard worldwide.
long_history: Dieter Doepfer began working with synth hardware in 1977, building a voltage-controlled phaser module for the Formant, a DIY analog synth kit published by Elektor magazine, and founded Doepfer Musikelektronik in Gräfelfing, Upper Bavaria in 1979. The company built a reputation for well-engineered, accessible electronics before its defining product: the A-100 modular system, unveiled at the 1995 Frankfurt Musikmesse and shipped from 1996, launched with around 10 module types and has since grown to well over 120. The A-100 fixed a set of mechanical and electrical standards -- 3U (128.5mm) panel height, module widths in multiples of 5.08mm (HP), and +-12V bus power -- that other manufacturers adopted as a de facto standard now known as Eurorack, today the most widely used modular synthesizer format in the world. Doepfer remains active and independently owned, continuing to produce Eurorack modules and other synth hardware.

short_history: Founded in 1971 in Santa Cruz, California by Dave Rossum, Steve Gabriel and Jim Ketcham (Scott Wedge joined soon after), initially building custom modular synthesizers before becoming an influential force in digital sampling. Its 1981 Emulator brought affordable sampling to musicians at a fraction of the cost of the Fairlight CMI, and later products included the SP-12 and SP-1200 drum samplers, a mainstay of early hip-hop production. Acquired by Creative Technology in 1993 and merged with fellow synthesizer maker Ensoniq in 1998, E-mu wound down as an instrument brand by 2002.
long_history: E-mu's engineers developed a digitally scanned polyphonic keyboard in 1973 that was licensed to both Oberheim Electronics and Sequential Circuits, whose Prophet-5 became the best-selling synthesizer built on the patent; through most of the 1970s this licensing income, alongside synthesizer IC chips co-developed with Solid State Micro Technology, funded the company more than instrument sales did. E-mu's own first products were the E-mu 25 (1971) and a modular synthesizer system, of which roughly 250 units were built for artists and universities. The Emulator (1981), priced at $7,900 against the Fairlight CMI's roughly $30,000, opened sampling to a much wider range of musicians, and was followed by the Drumulator, Emulator II and III, and the Emax series. The SP-12 and SP-1200 (mid-to-late 1980s) became foundational tools in early hip-hop production for their distinctive sampled drum sound. In 1990 E-mu introduced the ROM-based Proteus rackmount sound module line. Creative Technology (maker of Sound Blaster sound cards, not itself an instrument manufacturer) acquired E-mu in 1993, relocated it to nearby Scotts Valley, and in 1998 merged its instrument operations with Ensoniq, another synthesizer and sampler maker Creative had also acquired. From 2003 to 2007 the E-mu name was used for "Creative Professional" computer sound cards (the 0404, 1212m, 1616 and 1820 series) rather than instruments, alongside software such as Emulator X (2004) and Proteus X (2005), before the brand was wound down by 2002 as an instrument line in practice.

short_history: Electronic Dream Plant (EDP) was a small synthesizer manufacturer based near Oxford, England, founded in 1977 by musician Adrian Wagner together with electronics designer Chris Huggett. The company made its name with the Wasp, a cheap, brightly coloured monosynth with a non-mechanical touch keyboard that undercut the price of rival synths of the era. EDP expanded the line with the single-oscillator Gnat, the Spider step sequencer and the Caterpillar keyboard controller, but persistent financial trouble led Huggett to leave around 1980 and the original company to collapse into bankruptcy. Wagner kept the brand alive briefly through a follow-up venture before losing control of it in 1981, and the EDP name disappeared from the market by 1982. Decades later the Wasp's hybrid digital-oscillator and analog-filter design, and even its clunky touch keyboard, have inspired reissues and clones from other manufacturers.
long_history: EDP was set up in 1977 in the countryside outside Oxford by the musician and self-taught synth builder Adrian Wagner, who partnered with electronics engineer Chris Huggett to turn Wagner's idea for an affordable synthesizer into a sellable product. To get it into production, the pair secured roughly 10,000 pounds in backing from a London musical-instrument retailer, Argent's Keyboards. The result was the Wasp, unveiled in 1978 at the low price of 199 pounds, well under half what a comparable synth cost at the time. Its yellow-and-black striped case, borrowed from its insect-themed name, hid two digital oscillators feeding an analog filter, plus a keyboard with no moving keys at all: flat capacitive touch-plates under a printed sticker, an approach that saved money but proved fragile and unpopular with players used to a real keyboard action. Even so, the Wasp sold well enough that the first batch reportedly cleared out of a London shop within hours of going on sale in September 1978. EDP followed the Wasp with several siblings: the cheaper single-oscillator Gnat, styled by outside product designer Anthony Harrison-Griffin; the Wasp Deluxe of 1979, which added a proper mechanical keyboard and wood side panels; and the Spider, a 252-step digital sequencer built with the help of Oxford University engineer Steve Evans, unusually deep-featured for its time. A four-voice keyboard controller called the Caterpillar followed in 1980, though by then Huggett, after the company ran into serious money trouble in 1979, had already left. EDP subsequently went bankrupt as unpaid supplier debts piled up. Wagner tried to keep going under a renamed successor, Electronic Dream Plant (Oxford), which kept producing the Gnat, but he was pushed out of that venture too in 1981; he then set up a further small outfit, Wasp Synthesizers, that built a handful of wood-cased 'Special' editions of the Wasp and Gnat before folding within the year. The EDP name itself ceased trading by 1982. Huggett went on to found the Oxford Synthesiser Company that same year and later worked with Akai and, from the 1990s, Novation, where the 1992 Bass Station and its descendants explicitly drew on the Wasp's oscillator design. The Wasp's reputation has only grown since: its sound and touch-plate keyboard were cloned by hobbyists in the 2017 'Jasper DIY' project and, in 2019, given an affordable modern hardware remake by Behringer.

short_history: Electronic Music Studios (EMS) is a British electronic instrument maker founded in 1969 in Putney, London, by composer and engineer Peter Zinovieff together with composer Tristram Cary and electronics designer David Cockerell. The firm is best known for the VCS3, one of the first compact, commercially sold synthesizers in Europe, and for its portable siblings the Synthi A and Synthi AKS. EMS instruments became closely associated with British progressive rock and experimental music, turning up on records by Pink Floyd, Brian Eno and Roxy Music, and in the BBC Radiophonic Workshop's studio. Years of shaky finances pushed the original company into insolvency around 1979, after which its assets and manufacturing rights changed hands more than once. A small operation based in Cornwall, run since the late 1990s by a former employee, still builds instruments to the original EMS specifications today.
long_history: EMS traces back to a one-off electronic device Peter Zinovieff, David Cockerell and Tristram Cary built for composer Don Banks; its success convinced the trio to formally set up Electronic Music Studios (London) Ltd in Putney, London in 1969 to develop and sell instruments commercially. Their first product, the VCS3 (nicknamed 'The Putney'), launched later that year: a semi-modular synthesizer built into a small wooden case with three oscillators, a ring modulator, a joystick controller, and a distinctive pin-matrix patchboard instead of patch cables. At roughly 330 pounds it undercut Moog's competing modular gear by a wide margin and beat the Minimoog to market by about a year, making it one of the first synthesizers a working musician could realistically buy and carry. Cockerell was the main circuit designer, while Cary, already an electronic-music pioneer with his own home studio, shaped the instrument's L-shaped case and control layout; Zinovieff, who had earlier run the electronic group Unit Delta Plus with BBC Radiophonic Workshop members, drove the business side. EMS followed the VCS3 with the briefcase-portable Synthi A in 1971, the Synthi AKS in 1972 (which added a built-in sequencer and touch keyboard and became famous for its role on Pink Floyd's 'On the Run'), and the large-format Synthi 100 in 1971, a roughly 6,500-pound modular system of which only around 30 were built and which the BBC Radiophonic Workshop used heavily on programmes including Doctor Who. The company also built vocoders, sequencer modules, and even an early video synthesizer, the Spectron, in 1974. EMS gear found favour well beyond the classical and experimental scene it was designed for, turning up in recordings by King Crimson, The Who, Roxy Music, Kraftwerk, Tangerine Dream and Jean-Michel Jarre. Despite the instruments' cult status, EMS struggled financially for much of the 1970s; a costly, unsuccessful push into the mass market for guitar effects pedals is often cited as a contributing factor, and the company collapsed into bankruptcy around 1979. Its Putney and Great Milton operations were liquidated and manufacturing rights were picked up by Datanomics, a firm based in Wareham, Dorset, where some EMS production had already been happening since the early 1970s. Ownership and production continued to shift over the following years. In 1997 a former EMS employee, Robin Wood, acquired the rights to the EMS name and restarted small-scale production of the classic range built to the original specifications; that operation is now based in Ladock, near Truro, Cornwall, and continues to sell and service EMS instruments today.

short_history: Founded in 1998 in Gothenburg, Sweden by Daniel Hansson, Anders Gärder and Mikael Räim, who began the project a year earlier as a Chalmers University of Technology computer science course assignment. Its first product, the SidStation (built around the Commodore 64's sound chip), shipped in 1999, followed by the influential Monomachine in 2001 and a long line of sequencer-driven synths, samplers and drum machines (Machinedrum, Analog series, Digitakt, Digitone, Syntakt). Still active, headquartered in Gothenburg with additional offices opened in Los Angeles and Tokyo since 2012.
long_history: Elektron began not as a company but as a student project: in 1997, three computer science classmates at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden -- Daniel Hansson, Anders Gärder and Mikael Räim -- built a hardware synthesizer around the MOS 6581 sound chip from the Commodore 64 home computer as coursework. The project turned into a real product and the trio formally founded Elektron in 1998. Their first release, the SidStation, was built in a test run of just ten units in 1998 before reaching the public market in 1999; it remained in production until 2006, when the company's supply of vintage SID chips ran out. Elektron's commercial breakthrough came with the Monomachine in 2001, a digital synthesizer built around the company's now-signature deep sequencer, which established the workflow-focused design philosophy the brand became known for. Over the following two decades Elektron expanded into sample-based instruments (the Machinedrum and Octatrack), modern analog-hybrid grooveboxes (the Analog Four, Analog Rytm), and a more accessible compact product line (Digitakt, Digitone, Syntakt), building a reputation among electronic musicians for deep, performance-oriented sequencing rather than raw synthesis novelty. The company has remained headquartered in Gothenburg, where its research, development and production are based, and expanded internationally with branch offices in Los Angeles and Tokyo opened in 2012.

short_history: Elka was an Italian electronic organ and synthesizer manufacturer based in Castelfidardo, active from the 1960s through the mid-1980s and best known for its Rhapsody string-synthesizer line and the Synthex, a highly regarded eight-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer designed by independent engineer Mario Maggi and produced by Elka from 1981 to 1985. As a company more focused on home and combo organs, Elka never became a dominant force in the professional synthesizer market despite the Synthex's later cult status among electronic musicians. In the late 1980s Elka's business and instrument lines passed to General Electro Music (GEM), a fellow Castelfidardo instrument maker, which was itself consolidated into the Generalmusic group; from then on Elka survived mainly as one of Generalmusic's brand names rather than an independent company. Generalmusic's own financial collapse in the early 2010s, and a 2015 crowdfunding attempt to relaunch a Synthex reissue that failed to reach its funding goal, left Elka without any active production or official website today.
long_history: Elka's roots go back to Castelfidardo, one of Italy's historic centres for accordion and electronic-organ manufacturing, alongside contemporaries such as Farfisa, Crumar and GEM. Secondary, forum-derived sources describe Elka as founded around 1965, reading the name as an acronym combining 'Elettronica' and 'Kastelfidardo'; one such source names Mario and Piero Crucianelli plus two additional partners as founders, though this comes from a non-authoritative forum thread and could not be corroborated against a primary source, so it should be treated cautiously. Elka built home and combo organs through the late 1960s and 1970s, including models such as the Solist 505 monophonic synth, the Artist 707 and the X-705 combo organ and synth, and the Rhapsody string-synthesizer series, the Rhapsody 490 with a 49-key keyboard and two layerable voices and the larger Rhapsody 610 with 61 keys and four voices, built roughly between 1974 and 1980. Elka's best-known product, the Synthex, began as the independent creation of Milan-based designer Mario Maggi, who built a working prototype in 1981 after being turned down for backing by other Italian manufacturers including Crumar and GEM; he ultimately demonstrated the instrument to Elka executives through a chance introduction, and Elka agreed to fund and manufacture it. The Synthex launched at the 1982 Frankfurt Musikmesse, used a Rockwell 6502P CPU, eight-voice polyphony with two DCOs per voice, a built-in four-track sequencer, a multimode filter and a joystick for pitch and modulation instead of a wheel; roughly 1,850 units were built through 1985. It became popular with artists including Jean-Michel Jarre, who used it for the laser-harp sounds on 'Rendez-Vous', as well as Stevie Wonder, Depeche Mode's Martin Gore, Duran Duran's Nick Rhodes, Keith Emerson and film composer Fabio Frizzi. In the UK the brand was distributed as 'Elka-Orla' by a company called Bluebridge Music, which packaged Elka and the separate manufacturer Orla under one storefront name; Elka and Orla were never the same Italian legal company, and Orla, founded independently in Castelfidardo by Nazzareno Orlandoni, continued operating long after Elka's Italian operations ended. Elka's own instrument business was acquired by General Electro Music, another Castelfidardo maker, in either 1987 or 1989 depending on the source. GEM and Elka, along with a studio-equipment line called LEM, were later consolidated under the corporate name Generalmusic around 1994, which then marketed GEM, LEM and Elka as three separate brand lines. Generalmusic ran into serious financial trouble in the late 2000s, laying off staff in February 2009 and ultimately filing for bankruptcy around 2011. In December 2014 a Finnish group, Soundion Oy Ltd, took over ownership of the GEM, LEM and Elka brands and announced plans to bring back a product lineup in 2015 including a possible Synthex reissue; an Indiegogo campaign launched around July 2015 to fund that reissue failed to reach its goal, and no Elka products or official Elka website have surfaced since.

short_history: Founded in 1982 in Malvern, Pennsylvania by former Commodore/MOS Technology engineers Bruce Crockett, Albert Charpentier and Bob Yannes (co-designer of the Commodore 64's SID chip), after the trio left MOS over disagreements with its parent company. Ensoniq's 1984 Mirage brought digital sampling below $2,000 for the first time, and the company went on to build the ESQ-1, EPS, VFX and ASR synthesizer and sampler lines through the 1990s. Creative Technology acquired Ensoniq in January 1998 for $77 million, mainly for its sound-card technology, merged its instrument division with E-mu Systems, and wound down instrument production; the company was fully dissolved by 2002.
long_history: The founders initially traded as Peripheral Visions before adopting the Ensoniq name in 1983, and built their business around a custom Digital Oscillator Chip (DOC) that let them undercut rival sampler makers. The 1984 Mirage sampling keyboard, listed around $1,695 and often discounted further, was the first sampler to reach that price point, opening digital sampling to home and project studios rather than only professional facilities. Ensoniq followed with the ESQ-1 synthesizer, the EPS sampler line, and from 1989 introduced wave-scanning synthesis (an idea drawn from the far more expensive PPG systems) across its VFX and later models; the 1993 DP/4 was one of the first MIDI-controllable multi-effects units. Through the early 1990s Ensoniq competed directly with Japanese manufacturers Roland, Korg and Yamaha, and increasing competitive pressure and reported quality issues gradually pushed the company out of the instrument business. In parallel, Ensoniq diversified into computer sound cards in the mid-1990s (the Soundscape and AudioPCI lines, built on its own ES5503/ES5504/ES5505/ES5506/ES5548 chips), selling millions of units; it was this sound-card business, not the instrument catalogue, that motivated Creative Technology's $77 million acquisition of the company in January 1998. Creative merged Ensoniq's instrument operations with E-mu Systems, quickly discontinued the remaining synth models, and the Ensoniq name ceased operating by 2002.

short_history: Founded in 1962 in Tokyo as Keio Electronic Laboratories by Tsutomu Kato and Tadashi Osanai, initially producing rhythm machines and organs. Adopted the Korg brand and later the corporate name Korg Inc.; entered synthesizers in 1973 (Mini-Korg), with major success from the MS-20 and later Wavestation. Yamaha held a 51% stake 1987-1993 before founder Kato bought back control. Remains privately held and active, with a history of acquiring other audio-equipment brands (Vox in 1992, Darkglass Electronics in 2022).
long_history: Korg's roots trace to a Tokyo nightclub owner, Tsutomu Kato, who partnered with accordionist and engineer Tadashi Osanai in 1962 to build a better rhythm machine than the commercial units then available; their company began as Keio Gijutsu Kenkyujo, soon renamed Keio Electronic Laboratories and later Keio Giken Kogyo, named for the nearby Keio railway line. Their first product, the Donca-Matic DA-20 electro-mechanical rhythm machine, appeared in 1963, followed by a solid-state successor in 1966. In 1967 engineer Fumio Mieda joined the company and, after roughly 18 months of development, produced a programmable organ; the resulting product line was branded KORG (from Keio plus organ), and the company itself eventually took the same name. Concerned about competition in the organ market, Kato pushed the company into the emerging synthesizer category, releasing the miniKORG in 1973. Through the 1970s Korg built both affordable instruments for hobbyists and large patchable systems such as the PS series; co-founder Osanai died in 1977, and Kato continued leading the company alone. Yamaha acquired a controlling stake in Korg in 1987, shortly before Korg's breakthrough product, the 1988 M1 workstation, which sold more than 250,000 units and became one of the best-selling synthesizers ever made; despite Yamaha's ownership the two companies continued developing and marketing their instruments separately, even competing directly in the market. In 1989 Korg hired the design team let go by Sequential Circuits, then owned by Yamaha, and by 1993 Kato had bought back most of Yamaha's shares, restoring Korg's independence. Korg has since expanded well beyond synthesizers into digital pianos, samplers, drum machines, effects, tuners and software instruments, largely through acquisition: it bought the Vox amplifier and organ brand in 1992, saving it from a struggling parent company, and its current subsidiaries include ARP Instruments alongside Vox; in September 2022 Korg also acquired the bass-focused electronics company Darkglass Electronics. Founder Kato died of cancer in 2011, but Korg remains privately held and continues to release new instrument lines.

short_history: Founded in 1982 by inventor Ray Kurzweil, musician Stevie Wonder and engineer Bruce Cichowlas, growing out of Kurzweil's work adapting reading-machine technology for music. Its first instrument, the 1983 K250, was among the first synthesizers widely regarded as convincingly reproducing a grand piano's sound. Acquired by Korean piano maker Young Chang in 1990 (itself later acquired by Hyundai Development Company in 2006), Kurzweil has continued releasing flagship workstations, from the V.A.S.T.-powered K2000 (1991) through the K2700 (2021), and remains active today.
long_history: The company's instrument line traces back to Ray Kurzweil's collaboration with Stevie Wonder on reading-machine technology for the blind; a friendly wager between the two over whether a synthesizer could truly replicate a grand piano's sound became the starting point for Kurzweil's first instrument. The K250 (1983-84) was widely regarded as the first digital keyboard to convincingly emulate a grand piano. Young Chang, a Korean piano manufacturer, acquired the company in 1990; Hyundai Development Company acquired Young Chang itself in 2006, and in January 2007 Raymond Kurzweil returned to the company as Chief Strategy Officer. The K2000 (1991) introduced Variable Architecture Synthesis Technology (V.A.S.T.), establishing the K2xxx workstation line that continued through the K2600 (1999, with expanded effects) and later models, all supporting up to 8 GB of internal SCSI sample storage. The mid-1990s PCx series offered 88-key weighted MIDI performance controllers with four control zones, while the SP, Artis and Forte lines focused on sampled-piano stage instruments. The K2700, released in late 2021, continues the flagship workstation line with backward compatibility for K- and PC-series patches. Kurzweil has competed throughout its history with Korg, Roland, Yamaha, Clavia and Kawai Musical Instruments in the synthesizer and workstation market.

short_history: Founded in 1953 in New York by Robert Moog and his father as R.A. Moog Co., producing theremins. Introduced the first commercial modular synthesizer in 1964 and the Minimoog in 1970; renamed Moog Music in 1972. Sold to Norlin Musical Instruments in 1973, went bankrupt in 1987. Robert Moog's Big Briar reacquired the Moog trademark and revived Moog Music in 2002. Acquired by inMusic Brands in June 2023; still actively producing instruments in Asheville, North Carolina.
long_history: Robert Moog and his father founded R.A. Moog Co. in 1953, initially selling theremin kits from Trumansburg, New York, where Moog was studying engineering physics at Cornell. Moog began designing early modular synthesizer circuits around 1961 and introduced the first commercial modular synthesizer system in 1964, working closely with composers such as Wendy Carlos, whose 1968 album Switched-On Bach used Moog instruments and became a surprise commercial hit, briefly making the company profitable in 1969. The 1970 Minimoog, a compact, pre-patched synthesizer aimed at performing musicians rather than studios, became the company's most influential product and helped popularize the synthesizer as a mainstream instrument; the company was renamed Moog Music in 1972. Financial trouble led Robert Moog to sell the company and its trademark to Norlin Musical Instruments in 1973; Moog stayed on as a Norlin engineer with no real control over the products bearing his name, and left in 1977 to found a new company, Big Briar, in Asheville, North Carolina, initially focused on theremins and ribbon controllers. Norlin's Moog Music arm filed for bankruptcy in 1987. Robert Moog spent years working to recover commercial rights to his own name; by 2002 Big Briar had regained the Moog Music trademark and relaunched under that name, releasing the Minimoog Voyager the same year as its flagship reintroduction. Robert Moog died in 2005, but the company continued developing new instruments such as the Sub 37 (2014) and Subsequent 37 (2017). In June 2023 Moog Music was acquired by inMusic Brands, the audio-technology group that also owns Akai Professional, Numark and other music brands; Moog continues to design and build instruments at its original Asheville, North Carolina facility.

short_history: Founded in 1976 in Norwich, Vermont by Sydney Alonso and Cameron Jones, working with Dartmouth College composer Jon Appleton to develop what became the Synclavier, one of the first digital synthesizers. The Synclavier II (1980) combined digital synthesis, polyphonic sampling and, from 1981, hard-disk recording in a single system used by artists including Michael Jackson, Frank Zappa and Sting, though complete systems cost over $200,000 by the late 1980s. Unable to compete with cheaper MIDI synthesizers and personal computers, New England Digital closed in 1992; Fostex and AirWorks Media purchased its assets, and the Synclavier name continues through successor companies today.
long_history: The Synclavier began as the "Dartmouth Digital Synthesizer", developed from 1976 by Dartmouth students Cameron Jones and Sydney Alonso under composer Jon Appleton and professor Frederick Hooven; New England Digital Corporation was founded that year in Norwich, Vermont to bring the instrument to market, later relocating to White River Junction. The original Synclavier I (1977) was aimed mainly at university electronic-music programs as an alternative to expensive time-shared mainframes. Development accelerated in late 1978 and early 1979 when synthesist Denny Jaeger joined the team, and the commercially oriented Synclavier II debuted at the AES show in May 1980. In 1981 New England Digital pioneered recording digital audio directly to hard disk with its Sample-to-Disk option, years ahead of most competitors, and its Signal File Manager (SFM) software found use well beyond music, including U.S. military analysis of submarine acoustic signatures. The system's list of users included Michael Jackson, Frank Zappa, Pat Metheny, Sting, Genesis and Herbie Hancock, and its sound was distinctive enough that some concert halls reportedly banned it out of concern it would make musicians obsolete. By the late 1980s a complete Synclavier system cost upward of $200,000, and the combination of that price, an economic downturn, and rapidly improving affordable MIDI synthesizers and personal computers drove New England Digital to close in 1992. Fostex acquired assets for use in hard-disk recording systems, and AirWorks Media also purchased assets; the Synclavier trademark and software continue in use today through successor organizations.

short_history: British music-technology maker founded in 1992 by Ian Jannaway and Mark Thompson as Novation Electronic Music Systems; started with MIDI keyboard controllers, added the analog-modeled Bass Station synth in 1993, and became a Focusrite division after a 2004 acquisition.
long_history: Founded in High Wycombe, England in 1992 by Ian Jannaway and Mark Thompson under the name Novation Electronic Music Systems, the company's first product was the MM10, a battery-portable MIDI keyboard controller meant to pair with the Yamaha QY10 workstation. Its next release, the 1993 Bass Station, used digitally controlled oscillators to emulate a classic monophonic analog synth at an accessible price, establishing the brand in the synth market. Chris Huggett, previously known for designing the EDP Wasp and OSCar synthesizers, joined as technical director and shaped the company's instrument designs until his death in 2020. Through the late 1990s and 2000s Novation released the Supernova (1998), Nova (1999) and Supernova II (2000) synth workstations, then pivoted toward MIDI controllers with the ReMOTE and X-Station lines. In August 2004 Focusrite Audio Engineering acquired Novation, making it a subsidiary while it kept its own product identity. The 2009 Launchpad grid controller became one of the best-known tools in modern electronic production, and the company continued releasing instruments including the Circuit groovebox (2015), Peak synthesizer (2017) and Summit (2019). Novation instruments have been used by artists such as Orbital, Jean-Michel Jarre and Aphex Twin, the last of whom collaborated on the 2020 AFX Station.

short_history: Founded in 1969 in Santa Monica, California by Tom Oberheim, initially making effects and the Synthesizer Expander Module before releasing pioneering polyphonic synths from 1975 onward (Four Voice, Two Voice, later the OB-series). Went bankrupt in the mid-1980s and passed through several owners (including a company called ECC and guitar maker Gibson), with the Oberheim name later licensed to Italian organ maker Viscount in the 1990s. Gibson returned the trademark to Tom Oberheim in 2019, who now produces instruments again under the Oberheim name.
long_history: Oberheim Electronics was founded in Santa Monica, California in 1969 by engineer Tom Oberheim, who began by building effects units and the Synthesizer Expander Module (SEM) for other musicians before moving into complete instruments. Starting around 1975-76, Oberheim introduced some of the first widely available polyphonic synthesizers, the Four Voice and Two Voice, which pioneered the now-standard idea of a fixed pool of voice circuits allocated dynamically to played notes, and the company became a major force in synthesizers and drum machines through the mid-1980s with its OB-series (OB-X, OB-Xa, OB-8) and DMX/DX drum machines. The company's finances deteriorated in the mid-1980s, leading to bankruptcy and a chaotic period of ownership changes -- sources differ on the exact sequence and years, but the brand passed through a company known as ECC and was eventually acquired by guitar maker Gibson, which kept some Oberheim products (like the Xpander and Matrix-1000) in limited production and later attempted a revival with the 1994 OB-Mx. Gibson then shelved the brand and licensed the Oberheim name to Italian organ manufacturer Viscount, which released new instruments under the name in the 1990s, including the OB-12 virtual analog synth, before Viscount stopped making synthesizers around 1998. The Oberheim name then sat dormant under Gibson until 2019, when Gibson returned the trademark and rights to Tom Oberheim himself, who has since resumed producing instruments under his own name and the restored Oberheim brand.

short_history: The Oxford Synthesiser Company (OSC) was a short-lived British synth maker set up in 1982 by electronics designer Chris Huggett, fresh off the collapse of his previous company Electronic Dream Plant, together with Paul Wiffen. Its only product was the OSCar, a monophonic hybrid synthesizer combining digitally controlled oscillators with analog filters, distinguished by an unusual case wrapped in black rubber and designed by independent product designer Anthony Harrison-Griffin. Despite winning a devoted following among electronic and pop musicians for its distinctive additive-synthesis waveforms and eventually gaining MIDI, the OSCar could not compete commercially with cheaper mass-produced digital synths such as Yamaha's DX7. OSC shut down in 1986 after only a few thousand units had been built. The OSCar has since become a sought-after collector's instrument and lives on in several software emulations.
long_history: After Electronic Dream Plant folded, Chris Huggett founded the Oxford Synthesiser Company in 1982, reportedly with financial help from family, and brought in Paul Wiffen to help develop the new instrument. The result, the OSCar, reached the market in either 1983 or 1984 depending on the source. Unlike the Wasp's minimalist approach, the OSCar was built as a fuller-featured instrument: a 37-key, three-octave keyboard, two digitally controlled oscillators feeding a pair of switchable 12dB analog filters that could be linked for a steeper 24dB slope, and an unusual additive-synthesis mode letting a player shape custom waveforms by adjusting the levels of up to 24 harmonics directly from the keyboard. A built-in sequencer allowed limited duophonic playing by storing and replaying note sequences. Industrial designer Anthony Harrison-Griffin gave the synth its recognizable look: chunky black rubberized housing meant to protect the controls, a world away from the sleek finishes of Japanese rivals. Later production units, from around 1984 onward, added MIDI and an expanded 36-patch memory, up from the earlier 12 user and 24 preset slots. Around 2,000 OSCars are estimated to have been built in total before the company closed in 1986, unable to keep up with Yamaha's FM-synthesis DX7 and the broader shift toward cheaper digital instruments. In its short run, though, the OSCar found its way onto records by artists including Jean-Michel Jarre, Ultravox, Stevie Wonder and Asia, and it remained popular later with electronic acts such as Orbital, Underworld and Hardfloor. After OSC's closure, Huggett continued designing instruments, working on Akai's S-series samplers and then, from the 1990s, at Novation. The OSCar's legacy also lives on through software recreations such as GForce's impOSCar, and in 2024 Behringer announced a hardware clone under the name POLYOsc.

short_history: Palm Products GmbH (PPG) was a German synthesizer manufacturer based in Hamburg, founded in 1975 by musician and engineer Wolfgang Palm. After early modular and Minimoog-style monophonic designs, Palm pioneered wavetable synthesis in the late 1970s, a method of digitally storing and scanning through short waveforms to generate evolving timbres. That work culminated in the PPG Wave series (Wave 2, 2.2 and 2.3), which combined digital oscillators with analog filters and became widely used by new-wave and electronic artists through the 1980s. Falling prices for rival digital synths and samplers eroded PPG's market and the company ceased operating in 1987. Wolfgang Palm went on to help design wavetable instruments for Waldorf, a company founded by PPG's former German distributor, and in 2020 the PPG brand itself passed to the plugin company Brainworx and Plugin Alliance for use on software instruments.
long_history: Wolfgang Palm, a keyboardist active in the Hamburg music scene, founded Palm Products GmbH in 1975 to build electronic instruments, reportedly beginning with modular synthesizer gear supplied to acts including Tangerine Dream. His first standalone product line, the 300-series modular system, did not sell well, and he followed it with the more conventional, Minimoog-inspired monophonic 1002 and 1020 synthesizers; the 1020 stood out for using digitally controlled oscillators, which were more stable in tuning than the voltage-controlled oscillators typical of the era and gave PPG instruments a recognizable tone. Palm's most consequential work began in the late 1970s, when he developed wavetable synthesis, building up sound by digitally storing short waveform segments and smoothly scanning between them, first realized in the Wavecomputer 360 of 1979, an eight-voice polyphonic instrument pairing digital oscillators with analog filters and amplifiers. This technology matured into the PPG Wave 2 in 1981, followed by the Wave 2.2 and Wave 2.3 through 1987; roughly a thousand units across the Wave family were built in total, each oscillator offering dozens of selectable waveforms drawn from onboard wavetables. Priced around 7,000 to 10,000 dollars, the Wave series found favour with prominent 1980s acts including Depeche Mode, Gary Numan and David Bowie's collaborators, and Depeche Mode's Alan Wilder in particular became known as a heavy user. PPG also built companion computer hardware, notably the Waveterm from 1982, used to edit and design wavetables and sequences for the Wave synths, and around 1986 Palm prototyped an ambitious all-in-one workstation called the Realizer, which proved too costly and technically complex to bring to market. Increasing competition from cheaper digital synthesizers and samplers squeezed PPG's business through the mid-1980s and the company shut down in 1987. Wolfgang Palm did not leave the field: he contributed digital synthesis design work to Waldorf Music, a company founded in 1988 by PPG's former German distributor specifically to continue building wavetable-based instruments, starting with the Microwave, so that Waldorf's early products are widely regarded as PPG's direct technical successors. Decades later, in 2020, ownership of the PPG name and brand passed to the audio-plugin company Brainworx, part of the Plugin Alliance group, which began releasing PPG-branded software instruments; sources describe that deal inconsistently, naming either Plugin Alliance or Brainworx as the buyer, with Native Instruments later acquiring Brainworx.

short_history: Founded April 18, 1972 in Osaka, Japan by Ikutaro Kakehashi (previously founder of Ace Electronic Industries, a separate earlier company). Became a global leader in electronic musical instruments and drum machines (SH-1000, Jupiter-4, Juno-60, TB-303, TR-808, TR-909). Headquarters moved to Hamamatsu, Shizuoka in 2005. Taken private via a 2014 management buyout backed by Taiyo Pacific Partners; relisted on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2020.
long_history: Ikutaro Kakehashi founded Roland Corporation in Osaka on April 18, 1972, after resigning from his earlier company Ace Electronic Industries when its main investor was absorbed by an outside industrial firm; he started Roland with about seven staff and roughly $100,000 in funding. The name was chosen deliberately: short, easy to pronounce internationally, and starting with a letter not already claimed by rival manufacturers. Roland's first product was a rhythm machine, the TR-77, followed in 1973 by the SH-1000, the first compact synthesizer built in Japan, and the non-preset SH-3. The company expanded quickly into adjacent gear: the RE-201 Space Echo tape delay in 1974, the JC-60/JC-120 Jazz Chorus guitar amplifiers in 1975, and the semi-modular System 100 and modular System 700 synthesizers in 1976. In 1977 Roland released the MC-8 MicroComposer, one of the earliest microprocessor-controlled music sequencers. Kakehashi was also central to the creation of MIDI, working with Sequential Circuits' Dave Smith to standardize a common protocol among competing manufacturers, unveiled in 1983. Roland's later instruments, especially the TR-808 drum machine (1980), TB-303 bass synthesizer, and TR-909 (1983-84), became foundational to entire genres of electronic music including hip-hop, house and techno, well beyond their original design intent. The company listed on the Osaka Stock Exchange in 1989, and its headquarters moved from Osaka to Hamamatsu, Shizuoka in 2005. In 2014 Roland was taken private through a management buyout backed by Taiyo Pacific Partners, before returning to public markets on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2020. Today Roland's portfolio spans synthesizers, digital pianos, electronic drums, guitar amplifiers, effects units, mixers and DJ equipment, and includes the Boss brand for guitar effects and Roland DG for digital fabrication and printing technology.

short_history: Founded in 1974 in San Jose, California as Sequential Circuits by Dave Smith, whose 1978 Prophet-5 became the first fully programmable polyphonic synthesizer. Went out of business in 1987 and was bought by Yamaha; Smith continued under Dave Smith Instruments, which regained the Sequential trademark from Yamaha in 2015 and rebranded as Sequential in 2018. Acquired by Focusrite in 2021; still active today.
long_history: Sequential traces back to 1974, when engineer Dave Smith founded Sequential Circuits in San Jose, California, initially selling a 16-step analog sequencer module before moving into full synthesizers. The company's defining product was the Prophet-5, introduced in 1977-78: the first fully programmable polyphonic synthesizer, letting musicians save and recall patch settings instead of manually re-patching for every sound, and the first commercial instrument built around an embedded microprocessor. Sequential Circuits followed with other influential Prophet-series instruments through the early-to-mid 1980s, and Dave Smith was a central figure in developing MIDI, the technical standard that let electronic instruments from different manufacturers communicate, first demonstrated in 1983. Despite its technical influence, Sequential Circuits struggled commercially in the mid-1980s amid competition from cheaper digital synths, and the company folded in 1987, with Yamaha acquiring its assets and the Sequential trademark. Dave Smith went on to found Dave Smith Instruments, continuing to design synthesizers under his own name for over two decades, including the influential Prophet '08 and Prophet-6. In 2015, Yamaha returned the Sequential Circuits trademark to Dave Smith Instruments, and the company formally rebranded as Sequential in 2018, restoring the original name to its instrument lineup. Dave Smith passed away in 2022. In 2021, British audio technology group Focusrite acquired Sequential, which continues to design and manufacture synthesizers under the Sequential name.

short_history: Serge Modular is an American analog modular synthesizer system created by composer and engineer Serge Tcherepnin, developed together with Rich Gold and Randy Cohen at CalArts starting in late 1972. Tcherepnin hand-built the first roughly twenty units in 1973 and formally established Serge Modular Music Systems in California in 1974 to manufacture and sell the modules commercially, positioning them as a cheaper, more DIY-friendly alternative to Buchla and Moog systems. Production continued through the 1970s and into the mid-1980s, until Tcherepnin closed the original company in 1986 and returned to France. In the early 1990s the designs and production passed to Rex Probe's Sound Transform Systems, and since around 2015 the German company Random*Source has produced Serge modules in both classic 4U and Eurorack formats in collaboration with Tcherepnin himself, who since 2018 holds the title Chief Innovation Officer there.
long_history: Serge Alexandrovich Tcherepnin, born in 1941 near Paris into a family of composers, studied with Nadia Boulanger and at Harvard before working with Pierre Boulez and Karlheinz Stockhausen in the late 1960s. While teaching at CalArts under Morton Subotnick in the early 1970s, Tcherepnin worked with students Rich Gold and Randy Cohen to design a new kind of modular synthesizer aimed at being far less expensive than the Buchla systems used at the school; conceptual work began in late 1972 and the first roughly twenty hand-built units, informally called 'Tcherepnins', were assembled in Tcherepnin's home in 1973. After leaving his CalArts post in 1974, Tcherepnin set up a small manufacturing operation, first in Hollywood, to build the system commercially under the name Serge Modular Music Systems, with mass production ramping up from 1975. Unlike Buchla's approach of one dedicated function per module, Serge panels exposed raw circuit building blocks, using colour-coded banana jacks for control voltage, audio and gate signals, so that patchers could combine them in unconventional ways. The company relocated to a Victorian house on Haight Street in San Francisco around 1980, but sales declined through the early 1980s, and Tcherepnin closed Serge Modular Music Systems altogether in 1986, moving back to France; from 1986 to roughly 1993 modules were still built only occasionally, to special order. In the early 1990s Tcherepnin sold the circuit designs to Rex Probe, an early collaborator, who founded Sound Transform Systems in Oakland, California to resume regular production, later packaging modules into more approachable pre-built 'Shop Panel' and 'M-Class' systems; sources give either 1992 or 1993 for that transfer. Tcherepnin also non-exclusively licensed the Serge designs to several other manufacturers over time, including CGS and Elby Designs in Australia; the most prominent of these today is the German company Random*Source, which began building Serge modules in classic 4U and newer Eurorack formats around 2015 and now runs serge-modular.com as the current public face of the brand. Since 2018 Tcherepnin himself has again been formally involved as Random*Source's Chief Innovation Officer, working on what the company describes as a fifth generation of Serge modular hardware.

short_history: Siel (Societa Industrie Elettroniche) was founded in 1976 in Acquaviva Picena, in Italy's Marche region, by Carlo Lucarelli, an electronics designer who had previously worked at fellow Italian instrument maker Farfisa. Over the following decade the company built electronic organs and a well-regarded run of analog synthesizers, including the polyphonic Orchestra, the budget-friendly Cruise, and the six-voice Opera 6 and DK-series keyboards that added MIDI as the format matured. Some Siel designs were sold abroad under other brands, most notably as the ARP Quartet and the Sequential Circuits Prelude. The company ran out of money in 1986: it launched its last own-brand instruments that year and became insolvent, which is when Roland founder Ikutaro Kakehashi opened talks about taking it over. The takeover was completed legally in 1987, when the Siel company name was struck from the register and Roland Europe S.p.A. was entered in its place.
long_history: Siel traces back to 1976, when Carlo Lucarelli left Farfisa, another Marche-region instrument manufacturer, to start his own electronics firm in the small town of Acquaviva Picena in the province of Ascoli Piceno. This put Siel in the middle of a cluster of Italian keyboard makers active in the region from the 1950s through the 1980s, alongside Farfisa, Crumar, Elka, Bontempi, Eko and Welson. Siel's early focus was electronic organs, but by the late 1970s it had moved into synthesizers. Its 1979 Orchestra was a fully polyphonic, performance-oriented instrument built around a divide-down oscillator design with preset brass, string, reed/organ and piano voices; it proved influential enough that ARP Instruments licensed a version for the US market as the Quartet. A simpler monophonic model, the Mono, followed in 1980, and the 1981 Cruise combined elements of the Mono and Orchestra designs. In 1982 Siel revisited its flagship polysynth with the OR400 (Orchestra 2), a six-voice, two-oscillator-per-voice instrument that was among the first affordable polyphonic synths to offer velocity sensitivity and MIDI; Sequential Circuits distributed a rebadged version as the Prelude. Siel's best-remembered instrument is the Opera 6, an analog six-voice polysynth in the same market segment as Roland's Juno series, with later production runs swapping in DCOs for tuning stability and adding MIDI. The mid-1980s DK line (DK600, DK700, DK80, DK70) extended the Opera 6 architecture into splittable, layerable and dual-synth configurations, and Siel also built peripheral products such as the CMK 49 keyboard interface for the Commodore 64. The company's run as an independent maker ended in the second half of the 1980s. The two dates that circulate for Siel's end describe two different events rather than contradicting each other. 1986 was the operational end: the company presented its final own-brand models that year, among them the DK70 and EX70 synthesizers and the Keytek CTS-2000 built for Gibson, and became insolvent, at which point Ikutaro Kakehashi began negotiating a rescue and takeover. 1987 was the legal end: the acquisition was formally completed, the Societa Industrie Elettroniche S.p.A. entry was removed from the company register, and Roland Europe S.p.A. was registered in its place.

short_history: Teisco began in Tokyo in 1946 as a small electronics workshop founded by guitarist Atsuwo Kaneko and engineer Doryu Matsuda, going through two name changes before settling on 'Teisco Co.' in 1964. It became internationally known in the 1960s for inexpensive, distinctively shaped electric guitars, basses, amplifiers and drum kits exported to the US and UK. Piano maker Kawai acquired Teisco in 1967, wound the guitar business down over the following years, and in the late 1970s and early 1980s repurposed the Teisco name for a line of analog synthesizers such as the 100F, 60F, 110F and the four-voice SX-400, before retiring the brand. A separate, unrelated 2018 revival by BandLab Technologies brought the Teisco name back only for guitar effects pedals, not synthesizers.
long_history: Teisco's roots go back to 1946, when Hawaiian- and Spanish-guitar player Atsuwo Kaneko partnered with electrical engineer Doryu Matsuda to found a small instrument workshop in Tokyo, initially called Aoi Onpa Kenkyujo. The company was renamed Nippon Onpa Kogyo Co. in 1956 and finally Teisco Co. in 1964. Despite the name superficially reading like an acronym for 'Tokyo Electric Instrument and Sound Company', Kaneko himself reportedly said on record that this was not the origin, and that he simply liked how the name sounded. Through the 1950s and 1960s Teisco built a reputation, especially abroad, for affordable and unusually styled electric guitars, the palette-shaped 'May Queen' model being a well-known example, often loaded with four pickups and elaborate switching, along with basses including the six-string TB-64, amplifiers frequently badged 'Checkmate', drum kits and PA gear; production scaled up to tens of thousands of guitars a month at its peak, much of it OEM work for export markets including the US and UK, where players such as Hound Dog Taylor later used the instruments and where they found a second life in the 1990s among noise-rock and alternative guitarists as cheap alternatives to vintage Fenders. A downturn in the mid-1960s led Teisco to be acquired in 1967 by Kawai Musical Instruments Manufacturing Co., the Hamamatsu piano maker founded in 1927. Kawai ran Teisco largely as a separate operation at first, phasing out the Teisco name on guitars by 1969 in export markets and 1977 within Japan itself. Around 1977 to 1980, Kawai used the Teisco name for its first synthesizers, starting with the Synthesizer 100F, and expanded the range as Kawai pushed into overseas synth sales: the monophonic 60F and duophonic 110F arrived together, followed in 1981 by Kawai's first polyphonic synth, the four-voice SX-400, sold under the Teisco name outside Japan and sometimes as a Kawai-badged unit even within the same production run, since branding was inconsistent. By the mid-1980s Kawai had folded the Teisco brand entirely into its own name for keyboards. The Teisco name lay dormant for decades until 2018, when Singapore-based BandLab Technologies revived it, not for synthesizers or guitars but as a line of guitar effects pedals shown at that year's NAMM show; this revival is a distinct, present-day use of the name that falls outside the synth, organ and electric-piano scope of this database.

short_history: British organ and guitar-amplifier maker founded 1950 as the Jennings Organ Company; creator of the AC15/AC30 amps and the Vox Continental organ, famously used by the Beatles. Changed owners repeatedly after 1967 and has been Korg-owned since 1992.
long_history: Vox began as the Jennings Organ Company, founded by Thomas Walter Jennings in Dartford, Kent, England in 1950, initially selling accordions before developing its own instruments; its first notable product was the Univox, a mains-powered electronic keyboard with a built-in valve amplifier, similar in concept to the Clavioline. In 1956 employee and big-band guitarist Dick Denney showed Jennings a prototype guitar amplifier, prompting the company to rename itself Jennings Musical Industries (JMI) and pivot toward amplification alongside its organs. The 15-watt Vox AC15 launched in 1958, and Denney's follow-up design, effectively doubling the AC15's output with an extra speaker and cabinet, became the AC30 in 1959. Vox amplifiers became closely associated with British rock groups of the early 1960s, most famously the Beatles, after the band's manager negotiated free amplifiers in exchange for exclusive use; the Rolling Stones and other major acts of the era used Vox gear as well. Alongside amplifiers, Vox also produced electronic organs, including the Vox Continental, a distinctive reversed-color-key combo organ that became a signature sound of 1960s pop and rock. JMI's parent company, Royston, went bankrupt in 1967, and the Vox brand changed ownership repeatedly between 1967 and 1993, including a period under Rose Morris, which relaunched an AC30 reissue in the early 1990s. In late 1992 a struggling Rose Morris sold the Vox name to a new management team operating under the Korg umbrella; Korg, already the US distributor for rival amp maker Marshall in many markets, used that relationship to have Marshall manufacture new Vox-branded amplifiers under contract, stabilizing and modernizing the brand for the following decades. Vox remains a Korg-owned brand today, producing both guitar amplifiers and its historic line of combo organs.

short_history: Founded in 1887 in Hamamatsu, Japan by Torakusu Yamaha, who built the first reed organ made in Japan; incorporated in 1897 as Nippon Gakki Co., Ltd. Grew into one of the world's largest musical instrument makers, spinning off its motorcycle business as the separate Yamaha Motor Co. in 1955. Introduced the influential DX7 digital synthesizer in 1983 and briefly held a 51% stake in Korg (1987-1993). Still active today as Yamaha Corporation.
long_history: Yamaha's roots go back to 1887, when Torakusu Yamaha repaired a broken reed organ at a Hamamatsu hospital and, finding no local expertise to fix it, built one himself -- the first reed organ manufactured in Japan. He founded a workshop that grew quickly, employing around 100 people and producing roughly 250 instruments a year within two years. The company was formally incorporated in 1897 as Nippon Gakki Co., Ltd. ("Japan Musical Instrument Company"), and over the following decades expanded into pianos (its first upright in 1900, first grand piano in 1902), harmonicas, xylophones, and eventually a vast range of instrument families including guitars, brass, woodwinds, and strings, becoming one of the largest musical instrument manufacturers in the world. In 1955 the company spun off its motorcycle-manufacturing arm into a separately managed company, Yamaha Motor Co., Ltd. -- a well-known brand in its own right but a financially and organizationally distinct entity from the instrument-making Yamaha Corporation. On the electronic side, Yamaha became a major force in synthesizers, most notably with the 1983 DX7, the first commercially successful digital synthesizer, built on FM synthesis technology licensed from Stanford University -- its distinctive digital sound helped define the pop music of the mid-1980s. Yamaha also played a brief corporate role in Korg's history, holding a 51% stake in the company from 1987 to 1993 before Korg's founder reacquired control. Yamaha Corporation remains active today, headquartered in Hamamatsu, Shizuoka, Japan, and continues to manufacture instruments, professional audio equipment, and electronics.
